text: A business plan to support a strong collaboration in AI/ML for particle accelerator operations requires: • A clear set of priorities and well-scoped goals. • Champions in each organization with dedicated resources. • Upper-level management support within all participating organizations. • A decadal support modal that provides guaranteed funding and a corroborating usage model We propose two alternatives for a successful collaboration in accelerator operations, depending on im- mediate need. A third option exists and is discussed below, but would require additional discussion and legal frameworks, that would likely be insurmountable if collaborating between industry, academia and gov- ernment. In the future, these recommended models could be used to pivot ongoing projects, akin to how the WarpX and Xopt projects shifted ownership throughout their development. Due to open questions about data ownership and veracity for AI/ML models, there are significant legal and IP considerations that need to be ironed out. Additional options were considered, but several governance and funding models are incompatible with the partners and entities involved in accelerator operations or the long-term operation of large facilities. This is particularly true for collaboration models proposed by the National AI Task Force, which rely on NSF-style funding and assume the use of large-scale industrial compute infrastructure, such as Microsoft Azure or Amazon Cloud. Due to the physical infrastructure and network security requirements for accelerator operations and controls,theuseofcloudcomputingresourcesaretypicallynotapplicableforanythingbutdelayedprocessing and/or offline optimization paradigms. Control systems also generate a large amount of redundant data, contributing to high costs for offsite data movement and storage. While these challenges can in principle be resolved through systems analysis and design, the development of such techniques and infrastructure represent their own dedicated and facility-specific effort. 5.1 Option 1: Institution-home Leadership The most likely model to succeed would adopt many aspects of the NSF strategy, with the establishment of an AI/ML for accelerator operations research center with close ties to one or more extant facilities. This model has similarities to the previous organization of the US Particle Accelerator School, with direct buy-in and funding support from leadership at other accelerator facilities, while also allowing for the development of umbrella legal frameworks that do not limit the collaboration’s ability to work with others. Such a model would enable organic growth of software expertise and support across multiple institutions. As an example, SLACcouldserveasahostinstitutionforanAI/MLoperationsresearchlabthatleveragesexistingsupport ontheXoptprojecttoseedabroadermulti-institutionalresearchprogram. Subsequentcollaborativefunding efforts, analagous to SCIDAC, could provide dedicated long-term funding while also furnishing additional means for multi-institutional outreach and adoption. However, it would require an initial ‘seed funding’ period and multi-institutional coordination to provide the initial experimental data, simulation tools, controls interfacing, and model frameworks. Furthermore, implementing even this seed environment would require a data-sharing agreement from participating orga- nizations.
